turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mrs Briggs. We'll do your blood pressure before you go in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh, hello. I was sat out there ages, and I kept thinking, what if it's all gone wrong and—
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Coat sleeve up, please. Any coffee today?
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Half a mug, about half an hour ago. Does that ruin it? I read coffee sends it sky high, and I—
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): It can lift it a little. Sit quiet for me.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Sorry. Colin says I fidget. He's my husband, we live together. He's the diabetic one, not me.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): One hundred and fifty-two over eighty-eight. Pulse seventy-six, nice and regular.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): A hundred and fifty-two? That's worse, isn't it? Last year they said the cholesterol was borderline, not the pressure. I never got a printout.
[SEG0009] person_1 (NURSE): Doctor will have the notes. Any chest pain with the cuff?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I do go a bit light-headed some days, but that's separate, I think.
[SEG0011] person_1 (NURSE): He's free. In you go.
[SEG0012] person_3 (DOCTOR): Mrs Briggs. This is your high blood pressure review, and the cholesterol.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes, the blood pressure and the cholesterol. I've been worrying all week, honestly, because of something I read, and I need to tell you—
[SEG0014] person_3 (DOCTOR): Chest pain at all, in the last month?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0016] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any breathlessness walking on the flat?
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): No, I'm not breathless. The thing I read was about—
[SEG0018] person_3 (DOCTOR): Ankle swelling?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): No swelling. Sorry. I'll answer properly.
[SEG0020] person_3 (DOCTOR): You mentioned light-headedness to the nurse.
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. Two or three times a week. The room doesn't spin, I just go a bit floaty, and then it passes.
[SEG0022] person_3 (DOCTOR): Since when?
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): A couple of months, I think. Actually I can't say when it started. I keep trying to date it and I can't.
[SEG0024] person_3 (DOCTOR): Still on the ramipril?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure tablet, yes. Only I don't take it every day.
[SEG0026] person_3 (DOCTOR): The prescription is five milligrams, once each morning.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): I take five milligrams every other day. Some weeks I lose track and I'm not sure I've even managed that.
[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): And the cholesterol tablet — still taking that?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): The atorvastatin. I stopped it. I read this long piece online, about memory, and muscles, and I thought if I just—
[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Right. Start the atorvastatin again tonight, twenty milligrams, and I'll see you in six months. We don't need bloods. They were done last year.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Tonight? But I haven't told you—
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): When did you actually stop?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): It was the article that did it, pages of it, and then my neighbour said her sister came off hers and felt brighter, so I—
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): March. Or April. I honestly can't pin the day. I haven't swallowed one since.
[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): Dose before that?
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Twenty milligrams, at night. And my calves ached the whole time I was on it. That ache has gone, since I stopped.
[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Did you ever start the ezetimibe?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I never took that. The chemist was out, and I never went back for it, so it was never started.
[SEG0039] person_3 (DOCTOR): You mentioned Colin's tablets in the waiting room.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): His diabetes ones. Metformin, I think. They're his. I just see the box and I get in a state that I'll be next. I don't take them.

[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): They said my cholesterol was only borderline last time. I've had high cholesterol for years, and then they called that one borderline. Something like six, I don't remember the figure, and nobody wrote it down for me.
[SEG0042] person_3 (DOCTOR): Hold on. That changes the plan. I am not restarting the statin today, and scrap the six-month appointment.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): So I don't start it tonight?
[SEG0044] person_3 (DOCTOR): Correct. No atorvastatin until we have fresh bloods and we meet again.
[SEG0045] person_2 (PATIENT): What bloods? Will it be lots of tubes? I go shaky with needles, I should have said.
[SEG0046] person_3 (DOCTOR): A lipid profile and liver tests. You can have them in the next few days.
[SEG0047] person_1 (NURSE): Sorry to butt in. She's asking at the desk if those need to be fasting, and do you want me to add anything given the pressure was one fifty-two over eighty-eight?
[SEG0048] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fasting, yes. Add kidney function as well, because of the ramipril. Lipids, liver, and kidneys.
[SEG0049] person_2 (PATIENT): Fasting from when? I had coffee this morning, is today ruined? I can come back, I just need to know the rules, because I get it wrong and then—
[SEG0050] person_3 (DOCTOR): Not today. Nothing to eat or drink except water from midnight, the morning you come. Coffee today is irrelevant.
[SEG0051] person_2 (PATIENT): And I come back to you when?
[SEG0052] person_3 (DOCTOR): In a month. We'll look at the results and decide about a statin then.

[SEG0053] person_2 (PATIENT): What do I do with the ramipril between now and then? If I take it every day the floaty feeling might get worse, and if I fall Colin can't pick me up, he's not strong, and I—
[SEG0054] person_3 (DOCTOR): Take five milligrams every morning, including tomorrow. If the light-headedness gets worse, stop and ring the surgery. Don't space the days out yourself.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Even if I took one yesterday? I think I did. I'm not certain.
[SEG0056] person_3 (DOCTOR): Even then. Today's dose, then every morning.

[SEG0057] person_2 (PATIENT): Is there a chance the ramipril is causing the floatiness, not my age? I'm sixty-seven next month. My mum had a stroke at seventy. That's sitting in my head the whole time.
[SEG0058] person_3 (DOCTOR): It might be the ramipril. I can't be sure. Your mother's stroke matters. It doesn't mean we restart a statin blind.
[SEG0059] person_2 (PATIENT): So the stroke is family history, and Colin's diabetes isn't, because we're not blood. I did know that. I still ask.
[SEG0060] person_3 (DOCTOR): That's right. Mother's stroke counts. His diabetes doesn't.
[SEG0061] person_2 (PATIENT): If the calf ache comes back I can't work — well, I'm retired, but I walk his dog, and if I can't walk him—
[SEG0062] person_3 (DOCTOR): We can look at a different statin in a month if the lipids are up and the aches were real. Not before.
[SEG0063] person_2 (PATIENT): What if the lipids are fine? Can I stay off it for good? The article said lots of people don't need them if they're only borderline.
[SEG0064] person_3 (DOCTOR): I won't promise that. Borderline was their word, and you don't have the number. I won't treat a half-remembered result.

[SEG0065] person_2 (PATIENT): Porridge. I've been having it most mornings. Does that actually lower cholesterol, or is that another internet thing? And grapefruit. The article was obsessed with grapefruit.
[SEG0066] person_3 (DOCTOR): Porridge is reasonable. Grapefruit only matters if you go back on a statin. Leave it alone for now.
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): Should I be weighing myself? Nobody's weighed me. I feel heavier, but that might be the coat. Sorry, that's silly.
[SEG0068] person_3 (DOCTOR): No weight today. Not the decision we're making.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): And the blood form — three tests, lipids, liver, kidneys. If I turn up not fasting by mistake, do they send me away?
[SEG0070] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. They'll send you home to come back fasting. Don't do that.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): In a month even if I feel fine? Or only if something's wrong?
[SEG0072] person_3 (DOCTOR): In a month, either way. The appointment is booked as a plan, not a maybe.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): Reception can book the bloods and the month review on my way out?
[SEG0074] person_3 (DOCTOR): Yes. Bloods in the next few days, back with me in a month. No statin until then. Mind how you go.

spec.situation: Patient on routine review who admits stopping the cholesterol tablet after reading something online, still takes the BP tablet but 'every other day'; mentions husband's diabetes pills; doctor does not scold, plans repeat blood tests and revisits the statin decision in a month.
features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

stopped_or_never_taken: a medicine the patient stopped, was never given or only took once ('I stopped it in March'). Status discontinued, not current; a medicine never taken is not recorded as a medication.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.

omissions.text: Ramipril was prescribed as 5 mg once each morning; current recorded frequency of 'every other day' is nonadherent use rather than the prescribed regimen, and she sometimes is not sure she has even managed every-other-day dosing.
The patient denied chest pain specifically in the last month when asked by the doctor.
Light-headedness was described as 'the room doesn't spin', just feeling 'a bit floaty', then it passes.
Ezetimibe was never started because the chemist was out of stock and she never went back for it.

There was an initial plan to restart atorvastatin 20 mg tonight and review in six months, but the doctor then explicitly changed this plan: 'I am not restarting the statin today' and cancelled the six-month appointment.
The doctor said no bloods were initially needed because they were done last year, but then changed to ordering fresh fasting bloods (lipids, liver, kidney function) after hearing more history.
The planned blood tests were specified to be fasting.
The doctor advised not to space ramipril doses out herself.
The patient's age was stated as 67 next month.
The doctor said if lipids are elevated and the muscle aches were genuine, they could consider a different statin in a month rather than restarting atorvastatin now.

omissions.text: Ramipril adherence is recorded wrongly as currently used once each morning; the patient said she does not take it every day, takes 5 mg every other day, and some weeks is not sure she has even managed that.
Light-headedness has been present for a couple of months, though the patient could not date the exact start.
The patient denied chest pain specifically in the last month.
Atorvastatin was stopped because of concerns from an online article about memory and muscles, and the patient reported she had not swallowed one since stopping.
Ezetimibe was prescribed/considered but was never started because the chemist was out of stock and she never went back for it.

There was a real change in plan/disagreement: the doctor initially told her to restart atorvastatin 20 mg tonight and planned review in six months, then reversed this after hearing more history, cancelling that plan.
The doctor stated that blood tests were not needed initially because they were done last year, before changing the plan to obtain fresh bloods.
If lipid results are fine, the patient asked whether she could stay off statin for good; the doctor would not promise this and said he would not treat a half-remembered prior 'borderline' result.
The patient said she gets shaky with needles.
